msDesc.head: The Junius or Caedmon manuscript of Old English poetry. England; 10th century, second half or late, to 11th century, early or first half

summary.p: One of the four manuscripts which preserve the bulk of Old English poetry, and the only one to be illustrated. The manuscript is composed of two apparent textual units. Pages 1-212 were written by one scribe and contain the poems now known as Genesis (A and B), Exodus, and Daniel; pages 213-29 were written by three other scribes and contain the poem known as Christ and Satan. At p. 229 is 'finit liber .ii. amen' (in capitals); but there is no corresponding rubric for 'Liber I' either at the beginning of Genesis or the end of Daniel. (It may have appeared on a leaf now lost after p. 212.) The two textual units are made up of sections marked by larger initials and intermittently numbered in independent sequences. Pages 1-212 contain 55 sections; 'Liber II' is divided into twelve sections, four of which are numbered II, III, V, VI. Pages 213-229 also have some codicological differences from pages 1-212, described more fully below, but 'Liber II' cannot be considered a separate 'booklet'.

The relationship between the two textual units, and the question of the manuscript's textual and bibliographical unity, are controversial. Raw (1984) (partly following Ker 1957) argued that the final leaves of the last quire, following the end of Daniel, were originally blank, with drawings added soon after on pp. 225 and 230. Subsequently Christ and Satan - 'an afterthought, but a fairly early afterthought' - was added, partly on the existing leaves and partly on three added bifolia. An alternative interpretation is given by Hall 1986. The significance of a horizontal crease in the final pages of the manuscript is most recently discussed by Molinari 2014.

The literature on the manuscript is extensive and many points are controversial. The present description aims to give essential information on the manuscript's contents, codicology and history and to summarize the main contributions and areas of controversy. For further bibliography (to 2013) see Lockett 2013.

msItem.title: Genesis (Genesis A and Genesis B)
msItem.note: Lines 235-851 (pp. 13-40) are translated from an Old Saxon poem and have been edited separately as 'Genesis B', with lines 1-234 and 852-end edited as 'Genesis A'.

Text is lost at the following points:
Genesis A: after line 168 due to loss of leaves in quires 1 and 2; after line 234 due to loss of leaves in quire 2; perhaps also after line 205 due to loss of leaves in quire 2, depending on how the original quire is imagined (see Collation)
Genesis B: before line 235 due to the loss of leaves in quire 2; after line 440 due to the loss of two leaves after p. 22 in quire 3
Genesis A:
between lines 2381 and 2382 (loss of a leaf in quire 9 before p. 109); between lines 2418 and 2419 (loss of a leaf in quire 9 before p. 111); between lines 2512 and 2513 (loss of a leaf in quire 10 before p. 117); between lines 2599 and 2600 (lost of a leaf in quire 10 before p. 123); between lines 2806 and 2807 (loss of a leaf in quire 11 before p. 135). A leaf is lost in quire 8 before p. 95 without loss of text: presumably illustrations are missing.

supportDesc.support: parchment, generally arranged HFFH (Raw 1984 (p. 195) argues that a leaf is missing between pp. 212-213, where flesh currently faces hair)

116 leaves, paginated i-ii, 1-[230] by Junius
c. 325 c. 195
supportDesc.collation:
For the fullest description see Raw 1984; diagrams in Muir 2023.
1 (pp. i-ii, 1-8): a bifolium followed by three singletons.
2 (probably 8-6) (pp. 9-12): two singletons. The original arrangement of the quite is disputed: Raw (1984) and Doane (1991) pp. 33-34 present five alternative reconstructions. Pages 9-10 contain Genesis (A) 169-205 and pp. 11-12 contain Genesis (A) 206-234. Doane's preferred reconstruction necessitates a textual lacuna after line 205; Raw's does not.

9 (8-2), third and fifth leaves missing (pp. 106-116)

The two singletons may originally have been bifolia with the missing leaves (originally laves 5 and 9) also containing illustrations. See Muir 2023, 13-14 and 54.

layoutDesc.layout:
Ruled with a hard point several pages (probably a quire) at a time. Quires 1-7 (pp. 1-90) were ruled open (with the sheets flat). Quires 9-16 (pp. 105-210) were ruled folded with some re-ruling. (For quire 8 see below.) Pricked throughout in both inner and outer margins, except for pp. 219-222 (central bifolium of quire 17) and possibly pp. 217-8 and 223-4 (singletons in quire 17). Double vertical bounding lines on pp. 1-94 and 213-229; single on pp. 95-212.
The main exceptions are: quire 4, pricked for 28 lines but only 26 are ruled; quire 8 (pp. 91-104) is ruled with double vertical bounding lines to p. 94 and single lines thereafter; quire 17: pricking and ruling differ between pp. 211-16 and 225-29 (the outer three bifolia) and pp. 217-224 (the inner sheets). Raw 1984 (p. 201) concludes 'the three outer bifolia of quire 17 were pricked simultaneously and formed part of the original quire prepared for the end of Daniel'
Written space c. 225 c. 120 , with 26 lines per page, except for pp. 213-228, where the width is c. 135 mm, and there are 27 lines per page. Page 211 is ruled with 26 lines, but pricked for 27 lines.

handDesc.handNote: pp. 1-212: one scribe writing square minuscule with careful metrical punctuation.
pp. 213-229: three scribes writing vernacular minuscule, (1) pp. 213-215 (2) pp. 216-228 (3) p. 229.
A slightly later corrector or correctors altered spelling and punctuation on pp. 1-26 and 213-229, and added accents and hyphens throughout.

decoDesc.summary:
Illustration by two artists (pp. 1–68, and pp. 73–88). Artist B also illustrated the Cambridge Prudentius (Corpus Christi College MS. 23; Temple, no. 48) which was at Malmesbury by the mid-11th century but is likely to have been produced elsewhere. Decoration unfinished: on pp. 1-212 there are 48 extant illustrations, with 89 spaces for illustrations never completed. The three leaves (six pages) lost from the beginning of the manuscript may have contained up to six further full-page illustrations. The potentially missing leaves of 'Liber II' (see collation) may also have contained illustrations.
Pächt and Alexander iii. 34, pl. IV.
decoDesc.decoNote:
Scholarly debate has focussed on the model or models which the artists may have used (see in particular Raw 1976 and Broderick 1983), and the related question of the relationship between image and text, with many scholars (e.g. Henderson 1975) identifying moments of pictorial dislocation notably at pp. 20-24 and 76-78; see Karkov (2001), pp. 11-16 for a summary and an opposing view; also Doane (2013) 28-31. For metrical (?) inscriptions to some images, which Doane believes to be by the main scribe, see Old English Poetry in Facsimile. The following descriptions (based on Karkov pp. vi-ix and Ohlgren (1992) 88-99) are deliberately brief; for fuller detail and commentary see Ohlgren 1992 and Muir 2023, pp. 261-299.

Initials: pp. 1-73: zoomorphic initials (Type I) and one (p. 43) foliate initial. Generally replaced from p. 75 by plain initials, except at p. 79, p. 143 (the initial at the beginning of Exodus), and p. 226. The decorative initials are sometimes attributed to artist 1 of the illustrations, but see Lockett (2002) 149 n. 37.
Decorative designs often associated with the Ringerike style, pp. 225, 230.
Unfinished drawings, pp. 31, 96, added 12th century, second half (according to Pächt and Alexander).
Drawings in hard point and/or metalpoint of uncertain date (Ohlgren 1972).

additions.p:
As listed by Ker (1957), p. 407:
(a) xb 16 times, x 4 times, and xm once (see Gollancz, p. xxv, and Sisam 1953, 109)
(b) a medallion portrait on p. 2, entitled 'Ælfwine' (other scholars have disagreed as to whether this is an addition (e.g. Doane 2013) or by the first artist (e.g. Raw 1976)
(c) the words ‘healf trymt' (p. 98) and healf tmt' (p. 100), written in the main hand, interpreted by Ker as notes to remind the scribe that he had to leave the top half of p. 99 and of p. 101 blank (OE tramet ‘page’)
(d) scribbles in Latin on pages 164, 212, 214, 219 (see Gollancz, p. xviii) and the word 'innan' on p. 211.

binding.p: Romanesque binding of alum-tawed skin over oak boards, most fully described by Raw (1984) pp. 197-199. Three strap-and-pin fastenings now missing, except for a pin in the centre of the lower cover. Repaired probably in the second half of the thirteenth century as indicated by the script of pen trials on strips used to reinforce the binding using 'beaver-tailed' /S/. Formerly chained from the centre of the upper cover. M. R. James in 1903 recorded a 14th-century title 'Genesis' in capitals on the back cover, no longer visible (Ancient Libraries of Canterbury and Dover, p. xxv)

origin.origDate: 10th century, second half or late, to 11th century, early or first half
origin.note: Origin uncertain: arguments have been made for Canterbury (Temple, Doane (2013) pp. 32-5), Winchester (Ohlgren 1975, Fox 2002, Johnson 2020) and Malmesbury (Lucas 1980, to which Thomson 1982 responds).

The script of pp. 1-212 was dated "s. x/xi" by Ker. The most detailed discussion of palaeographical, art-historical and codicological evidence for dating of pp. 1-212 is Lockett (2002) which argues for c. 960 - c. 990l; see also Stokes (2014) 127-129. Ker dated pp. 213-229 to the first half of the eleventh century. For the suggestion that the Ælfwine portrayed on p. 2 was the patron of the manuscript, see for example Raw (1976) 135.

history.provenance: Canterbury, Kent, Benedictine cathedral priory of Holy Trinity or Christ Church (?) : perhaps identical with 'Genesis anglice depicta' in the catalogue of Prior Eastry, early 14th century: James, Ancient Libraries ... , pp. xxv, 509.(MLGB: inferred evidence). It has been argued that the manuscript was part of the 'corpus of Canterbury material that influenced the designer of the Bayeux tapestry' (Lewis 2011 at p. 111).

Sir Simonds D'Ewes (?). MS. Junius 11 was transcribed by William Somner who headed the transcription with two inscriptions written at different times: (1) "transcriptum a pervetusto libro MS in in bibliotheca Duvesiana ..." (2) " ad RR archip. Armachan ... liber spectat et penes eum est". This may mean either that Ussher lent the manuscript to D'Ewes, or that the manuscript belonged to D'Ewes and passed from him to Ussher. Other manuscripts did pass from D'Ewes to Ussher but there is no other evidence that D'Ewes owned MS. Junius 11. See Andrew G. Watson, The Library of Sir Simonds D'Ewes (London, 1976), pp. 9-10.

James Ussher (1581–1656), archbishop of Armagh. Ussher seems to have lent the manuscript to Johannes de Laet who used it in the 1640s as a source for a dictionary of Old English (Karkov, p. 182). The manuscript was given by Ussher by 1652 to:
Franciscus Junius, who edited the poems in 1655.
history.acquisition: Bequeathed by Junius to the Bodleian and received by by 1677.
